label: def:rooted_network
title: Definition
body_md: \label{def:rooted_network}A \emph{(binary) rooted (phylogenetic) network} on~$\mathcal{X}$ is a rooted, directed acyclic graph~$N^+$ such that (i) the root has indegree zero and outdegree two; (ii) the leaves have indegree one, outdegree zero and they are bijectively labeled by $\mathcal{X}$; (iii) all other vertices either have indegree one and outdegree two, or indegree two and outdegree one.
head: environment
name: Rooted network

label: def:semi_directed
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:semi_directed}
A \emph{(binary) semi-directed (phylogenetic) network} on~$\mathcal{X}$ is a mixed graph~$N$ that can be obtained from a rooted LSA network~$N^+$ on~$\mathcal{X}$ by undirecting all non-reticulation edges and, exhaustively, identifying parallel edges, suppressing degree-2 vertices, and suppressing 2-blobs until this is no longer possible.
head: environment
name: Semi-directed network

label: def:restriction
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:restriction}
Given a semi-directed network $N$ on $\mathcal{X}$ and some $\mathcal{Y} \subseteq \mathcal{X}$ with $| \mathcal{Y} | \geq 2$, the \emph{subnetwork} of $N$ induced by $\mathcal{Y}$ is the semi-directed network $N|_\mathcal{Y}$ on $\mathcal{Y}$ obtained from $N$ by taking the union of all up-down paths between leaves in $\mathcal{Y}$, followed by exhaustively identifying parallel edges, suppressing degree-2 vertices, and suppressing 2-blobs until this is no longer possible.
head: environment
name: Subnetwork

label: def:generator
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:generator}
    A mixed (resp. directed) multi-graph~$G$ is a \emph{level-$k$, semi-directed} (resp. \emph{rooted}) \emph{generator} for some integer $k\geq 1$ if $G$ is isomorphic to the generator of a simple, strictly level-$k$, semi-directed (resp. rooted) network.
head: environment
name: Generator

label: prop:semidirecting_rooted_generators
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:semidirecting_rooted_generators}
    A mixed multi-graph~$G$ is a level-$k$, semi-directed generator for some integer $k\geq 2$ if and only if it can be obtained by semi-directing some level-$k$, rooted generator $G^+$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let~$G$ be a level-$k$, semi-directed generator and let $N$ be a simple, level-$k$, semi-directed network such that $G \cong \mathrm{gen}(N)$. By definition, there also exists a rooted network~$N^+$ from which $N$ can be obtained by performing the operations in \cref{def:semi_directed}. In particular, we can obtain one such network $N^+$ by subdividing a single edge in the `source component'\footnote{Informally speaking, the source component of a semi-directed network is the set of vertices and edges that can be selected as the root of the network. Since this concept of a source component is technical and not needed elsewhere in the paper, we refer to \cite{holtgrefe2026characterizing} for a formal definition.} of $N$ to create a root~$\rho$ and then orienting all edges away from it~\cite{holtgrefe2026characterizing}. Consequently, $G$ and $G^+ = \mathrm{gen} (N^+)$ have the exact same vertex set, except for the addition of an outdegree-2 vertex (which corresponds to~$\rho$) in $G^+$. Moreover, each reticulation side of $G$ corresponds to exactly one reticulation side in $G^+$. Thus, semi-directing $G^+$ yields~$G$.

Conversely, suppose that $G$ is a mixed multi-graph that can be obtained by semi-directing some level-$k$, rooted generator $G^+$. Let $N^+$ be a rooted network with root~$\rho$ such that $\mathrm{gen} (N^+) \cong G^+$. Note that we may choose $N^+$ such that it has at least one leaf attached to every side. Consequently, when performing the operations of \cref{def:semi_directed} to obtain the corresponding semi-directed network~$N$, no parallel edges will appear after suppressing the root~$\rho$. Hence, $N$ only differs from $N^+$ by the suppression of~$\rho$ and the non-reticulation edges being undirected. An argument similar to that in the previous paragraph can then be used to show  that by construction $\mathrm{gen} (N) \cong G$.
head: environment

label: cor:generator_size_bound
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:generator_size_bound}
A level-$k$, semi-directed generator, $k\geq 1$, has at most $3k-2$ vertices and $4k-3$ edges.
head: environment

label: obs:level_cruciality
title: Observation
body_md:
\label{obs:level_cruciality}
Let $N$ be a simple, level-$k$, semi-directed network. Then, the cruciality of $N$ is at most~$k$.
head: environment

label: obs:cruciality_parallel_edges
title: Observation
body_md:
\label{obs:cruciality_parallel_edges}
    Let $N$ be a simple, semi-directed network whose generator has a pair of parallel edge sides. Then, the cruciality of $N$ is at least~2.
head: environment

label: prop:tree_of_blobs_encoding
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:tree_of_blobs_encoding}
    Let $N_1$ and $N_2$ be two semi-directed networks on~$\mathcal{X}$ and let $T_1$ and $T_2$ be their respective trees-of-blobs. If $\mathcal{S}_4 (N_1 ) \simeq \mathcal{S}_4 (N_2)$, then $T_1 \cong T_2$.
head: environment
name: Cor.\,5.6\

label: prop:crucial_leaves
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{prop:crucial_leaves}
Let $N$ be a simple, semi-directed network on $\mathcal{X}$ and let $\mathcal{Y} \subseteq \mathcal{X}$ with $|\mathcal{Y}| \geq 3$. Then, $\mathcal{Y} \subseteq \mathcal{X}$ is a set of crucial leaves of $N$ if and only if $N|_{\mathcal{Y}}$ is simple and $\mathrm{gen} (N) \cong \mathrm{gen} (N|_{\mathcal{Y}})$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathcal{Y}$ be a set of crucial leaves of $N$ and set $\mathcal{Z} = \mathcal{X} \setminus \mathcal{Y}$. We show that $N|_{\mathcal{Y}}$ is simple and $\mathrm{gen}(N) \cong \mathrm{gen}(N|_{\mathcal{Y}})$ by repeatedly removing leaves in $\mathcal{Z}$. This is trivial if $\mathcal{Z} = \emptyset$, so take any $x \in \mathcal{Z}$. Since $x \notin \mathcal{Y}$, it is neither attached to a reticulation side nor the unique leaf attached to a pair of parallel edge sides. Thus, constructing $N|_{\mathcal{X} \setminus \{x\}}$ from $N$ amounts solely to deleting the leaf~$x$ and suppressing a degree-2 vertex, keeping the network simple and leaving the generator unchanged. Moreover, the leaves in $\mathcal{Y}$ form a set of crucial leaves of $N|_{\mathcal{X} \setminus \{x\}}$. Repeating this procedure for every leaf in $\mathcal{Z}$ yields $N|_{\mathcal{Y}}$ while keeping the network simple and preserving the generator throughout. Hence, $N|_{\mathcal{Y}}$ is simple and $\mathrm{gen}(N) \cong \mathrm{gen}(N|_{\mathcal{Y}})$.

    Conversely, suppose that~$\mathcal{Y}$ is not a crucial leaf set of $N$. Then, there is either a reticulation side or a pair of parallel edge sides with no attached leaf in~$\mathcal{Y}$. In the first case, it is clear that $N|_{\mathcal{Y}}$ has at least one reticulation vertex fewer than~$N$. Since we identify parallel edges in the construction of $N|_{\mathcal{Y}}$ (\cref{def:restriction}), a similar argument applies in the second case. It follows that $N|_{\mathcal{Y}}$ has a strictly lower level than $N$. Thus, either $N|_{\mathcal{Y}}$ is not simple, or, if it is, $\mathrm{gen} (N) \not \cong \mathrm{gen} (N|_{\mathcal{Y}})$.
head: environment

label: cor:generator_encoding
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $r_1$ (resp. $r_2$) be the number of reticulations of $N_1$ (resp. $N_2$). Assume without loss of generality that $r_1 \geq r_2$. Let $\mathcal{Y} \subseteq \mathcal{X}$ be a smallest set of crucial leaves of $N_1$ and note that $|\mathcal{Y} | \leq k$. 
    
    By \cref{prop:crucial_leaves}, $\mathrm{gen} (N_1) \cong \mathrm{gen} (N_1|_{\mathcal{Y}} )$. Since $\mathcal{S}_k (N_1 ) \simeq\mathcal{S}_k (N_2)$, we have $N_1|_\mathcal{Y} \cong N_2|_\mathcal{Y}$, and so $\mathrm{gen} (N_1|_\mathcal{Y}) \cong \mathrm{gen} (N_2|_\mathcal{Y} )$. Thus, $\mathrm{gen} (N_1) \cong \mathrm{gen} (N_2|_\mathcal{Y} )$ and both have $r_1$ reticulations. Observe that $N_2|_{\mathcal{Y}}$ can have at most $r_2$ reticulations, since constructing a subnetwork never creates reticulations. By assumption, we also have $r_1 \geq r_2$, so $N_2|_\mathcal{Y}$ and $N_2$ have the same number of reticulations. It follows that $\mathcal{Y}$ is a set of crucial leaves of $N_2$ (see the proof of \cref{prop:crucial_leaves}), and thus $\mathrm{gen} (N_2|_\mathcal{Y} ) \cong \mathrm{gen} (N_2 )$ by \cref{prop:crucial_leaves}, proving the result.
head: environment

label: lem:equivalence_class_encoding
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cref{cor:generator_encoding}, we may assume $\mathrm{gen} (N_1) \cong \mathrm{gen} (N_2)$. Towards a contradiction, assume that $N_1$ and $N_2$ are not leaf-side consistent. Let $x \in \mathcal{X}$ be such that $\sigma_{N_1} (x) 
eq \sigma_{N_2} (x)$. Let $\mathcal{Y} \subseteq \mathcal{X}$ be a set of $k$ crucial leaves of $N_1$ and let $\mathcal{Z} =\mathcal{Y} \cup \{ x\}$. Since $\mathcal{S}_{k+1} (N_1 ) \simeq \mathcal{S}_{k+1} (N_2)$, we have $N_1|_\mathcal{Z} \cong N_2|_\mathcal{Z}$, so $\mathrm{gen} (N_1|_{\mathcal{Z}}) \cong \mathrm{gen} (N_2|_{\mathcal{Z}})$. By \cref{prop:crucial_leaves}, $\mathrm{gen} (N_1) \cong \mathrm{gen} (N_1|_{\mathcal{Z}})$. Therefore, $N_1$, $N_2$, $N_1|_\mathcal{Z}$ and $N_2|_\mathcal{Z}$ all have the same generator.
    But since $\sigma_{N_1} (x) 
eq \sigma_{N_2} (x)$, we get $\sigma_{N_1|_{\mathcal{Z}}} (x) 
eq \sigma_{N_2|_{\mathcal{Z}}} (x)$. So, $N_1|_{\mathcal{Z}} 
ot \cong N_2|_{\mathcal{Z}}$: a contradiction.
head: environment

label: lem:share_sides
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{lem:share_sides}
    Let $N_1$ and $N_2$ be two simple, $k$-crucial, semi-directed networks on $\mathcal{X}$. Let $x, y \in \mathcal{X}$. Suppose that one of the following holds.
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \looseness = -1
        \item $\mathcal{S}_{k+2} (N_1 ) \simeq \mathcal{S}_{k+2} (N_2)$; or
        \item $\mathcal{S}_{k+1} (N_1 ) \simeq \mathcal{S}_{k+1} (N_2)$ and $x$ is attached to a parallel edge side in $N_1$.
    \end{enumerate}
    Then $x$ and $y$ share a side in $N_1$ if and only if they share a side in $N_2$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First suppose that $\mathcal{S}_{k+2} (N_1 ) \simeq \mathcal{S}_{k+2} (N_2)$. By \cref{cor:generator_encoding} we may assume that $N_1$ and $N_2$ have the same generator.
    Let $\mathcal{Y} \subseteq \mathcal{X}$ be a set of $k$ crucial leaves of $N_1$ and let $\mathcal{Z} = \mathcal{Y} \cup \{x, y\}$. Since $\mathcal{S}_{k+2} (N_1 ) \simeq \mathcal{S}_{k+2} (N_2)$, we have that $N_1|_\mathcal{Z} \cong N_2|_\mathcal{Z}$, so $\mathrm{gen} (N_1|_\mathcal{Z}) \cong \mathrm{gen} (N_2|_\mathcal{Z})$. 
                                                                
    By \cref{prop:crucial_leaves}, we obtain $\mathrm{gen} (N_1) \cong \mathrm{gen} (N_1|_\mathcal{Z})$. Therefore, $N_1$, $N_2$, $N_1|_\mathcal{Z}$ and $N_2|_\mathcal{Z}$ all have isomorphic generators. It follows that $x$ and $y$ share a side in $N_1$ if and only if they share a side in $N_1|_\mathcal{Z} \cong N_2|_\mathcal{Z}$ if and only if they share a side in $N_2$. This proves the proposition in case (a) holds. If (b) holds, observe that we can choose $\mathcal{Y}$ such that $x \in \mathcal{Y}$.
head: environment

label: lem:excellent_original
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:excellent_original}
Let $N$ be a simple, semi-directed network on $\mathcal{X}$ that is not a phylogenetic tree. Let~$e$ be an edge of~$N$ between two non-leaf vertices. Then~$e$ is contained in at least one excellent cycle.
head: environment
name: Lem.\,5.4

label: lem:excellent_cycle
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:excellent_cycle}
    Let $N$ be a simple, semi-directed network on $\mathcal{X}$ that is not a phylogenetic tree. Let $\mathcal{Y} \subsetneq \mathcal{X}$ be a set of leaves that share an edge side. Then, there exists a leaf $z \in \mathcal{X} \setminus \mathcal{Y}$ that is attached to a reticulation side such that $N|_{\mathcal{Y} \cup \{z\}}$ is simple.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $m = |\mathcal{Y}| + 1$. 
    Let $e$ be one of the edges of $N$ that corresponds to the edge side to which the leaves in~$\mathcal{Y}$ are attached. Observe that $e$ is not a cut-edge. By \cref{lem:excellent_original}, it 
    follows that $e$ is contained in at least one excellent cycle~$C$. Let~$z$ be the leaf adjacent to the sink of this cycle.
    By Theorem~2 of \cite{holtgrefe2026characterizing} outlined above, (i) $C$ is not a semi-directed cycle; and (ii) no set of undirected edges contained in~$C$ forms a path in $N$ between two reticulations. Hence, all edges in $C$ are on an up-down path between two leaves in $\mathcal{Y} \cup \{z\}$. Letting $V(C)$ denote the vertex set of $C$
    and observing that all leaves in $\mathcal{Y} \cup \{z\}$ are adjacent to distinct vertices of~$V(C)$, it follows that $N|_{\mathcal{Y} \cup \{z\}}$ contains an $m$-blob. Since $N|_{\mathcal{Y} \cup \{z\}}$ also has $m$ leaves, it follows that $N|_{\mathcal{Y} \cup \{z\}}$ is simple.
head: environment

label: lem:ordering
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{lem:ordering}
    Let $N_1$ and $N_2$ be two simple, $k$-crucial, semi-directed networks on~$\mathcal{X}$ with the same generator~$G$. Let $\mathcal{Y} \subseteq \mathcal{X}$ be a set of leaves that all share the same edge side $S = uv$ of $G$ in both $N_1$ and $N_2$.
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
        \item If $\mathcal{S}_{4} (N_1) \simeq \mathcal{S}_4 (N_2)$, then the unoriented ordering of~$\mathcal{Y}$ induced by~$S$ is the same in $N_1$ and $N_2$.
        \item If $\mathcal{S}_{k+2} (N_1) \simeq \mathcal{S}_{k+2} (N_2)$ and $S$ is oriented, then the $uv$-oriented ordering of~$\mathcal{Y}$ induced by~$S$ is the same in $N_1$ and $N_2$.
        \item If $\mathcal{S}_{k+1} (N_1) \simeq \mathcal{S}_{k+1} (N_2)$ and $S$ is a parallel edge side, then the $uv$-oriented ordering of~$\mathcal{Y}$ induced by~$S$ is the same in $N_1$ and $N_2$.
    \end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(a): Suppose $\mathcal{S}_{4} (N_1) \simeq \mathcal{S}_4 (N_2)$. Observe that there is only one possible unoriented ordering of~$\mathcal{Y}$ if $|\mathcal{Y}| \leq 2$, so we may assume $|\mathcal{Y} | \geq 3$. Let $\mathcal{Y}' \subseteq \mathcal{Y}$ be an arbitrary subset of $\mathcal{Y}$ with $|\mathcal{Y}'| = 3$. By \cref{lem:excellent_cycle}, there is a leaf $z \in \mathcal{X} \setminus \mathcal{Y}$ that is attached to a reticulation side of~$G$ such that $N_1|_\mathcal{Z}$, with $\mathcal{Z} =\mathcal{Y}' \cup \{z\}$, is simple. Since $\mathcal{S}_{4} (N_1) \simeq \mathcal{S}_4 (N_2)$, $N_2|_\mathcal{Z}$ is also simple. Let $i \in \{1, 2\}$. Clearly, the leaves in~$\mathcal{Y}'$ share a side in $N_i|_\mathcal{Z}$ because they shared a side in $N_i$. Moreover, the induced unoriented ordering of $\mathcal{Y}'$ in $N_i|_\mathcal{Z}$ is the same as the induced unoriented ordering of $\mathcal{Y}'$ in $N_i$. Because $\mathcal{S}_{4} (N_1) \simeq \mathcal{S}_4 (N_2)$, these orderings are also the same across $N_1$ and $N_2$. The result follows from the fact that the unoriented ordering of~$\mathcal{Y}$ is fully determined by the unoriented orderings of all its size-3 subsets of leaves.

    (b): Suppose $\mathcal{S}_{k+2} (N_1) \simeq \mathcal{S}_{k+2} (N_2)$ and that $S$ is oriented. The result is trivial if $|\mathcal{Y}| =1$, so we assume $|\mathcal{Y}| \geq 2$. Let $\mathcal{Y}' \subseteq \mathcal{Y}$ be an arbitrary subset of $\mathcal{Y}$ with $|\mathcal{Y}'|=2$ and let $C \subseteq \mathcal{X}$ be some smallest set of crucial leaves of $N_1$. By \cref{lem:equivalence_class_encoding}, $N_1$ and $N_2$ are leaf-side consistent, so $C$ is also a set of crucial leaves of $N_2$. Let $\mathcal{Z} = C \cup \mathcal{Y}'$. Then, since $N_i$ and $N_i|_\mathcal{Z}$ have the same generator, the $uv$-oriented ordering of $\mathcal{Y}'$ in $N_i|_\mathcal{Z}$ equals the $uv$-oriented ordering of $\mathcal{Y}'$ in $N_i$, for $i \in \{1, 2\}$. Observe that $|\mathcal{Z}| \leq k+ 2$. So, by our assumption, $N_1|_\mathcal{Z} \cong N_2|_\mathcal{Z}$ and thus these $uv$-oriented orderings of $\mathcal{Y}'$ also coincide across $N_1$ and $N_2$. The result follows by noting that the $uv$-oriented ordering of~$\mathcal{Y}$ is fully determined by the $uv$-oriented orderings of all its size-2 subsets of leaves.

    (c): First note that parallel edge sides are directed and therefore oriented. Observe that in the proof of Part~(b), we can pick a set of crucial leaves $C \subseteq \mathcal{X}$ that contains a leaf from $\mathcal{Y}'$ if $S$ is a parallel edge side. Then, $|\mathcal{Z}| \leq k + 1$. The remainder of the proof is similar to the proof of Part~(b).
head: environment

label: lem:backbone
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:backbone}
    Let $N_1$ and $N_2$ be two simple, $k$-crucial, semi-directed networks on $\mathcal{X}$ with the same generator~$G$ having parallel edge sides. If $\mathcal{S}_{k+1} (N_1 ) \simeq \mathcal{S}_{k+1} (N_2)$, then $N_1$ and $N_2$ have isomorphic backbones.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $N^b_i$ be the backbone of $N_i$, $ i \in \{1, 2\}$. Note that this backbone exists, since a network whose generator contains parallel edge sides has a cruciality of at least~2 (\cref{obs:cruciality_parallel_edges}). Because the leaf set of $N^b_i$ is a crucial leaf set of $N_i$ by construction, it follows from \cref{prop:crucial_leaves} that $N^b_i$ also has $G$ as its generator.
Next, note that a pair of parallel edge sides always forms its own side-equivalence class. Similarly, a reticulation side forms its own side-equivalence class.
Since~$N_1$ and $N_2$ are leaf-side consistent (\cref{lem:equivalence_class_encoding}), the two networks then share the same set of leaves on each pair of parallel edge sides and on each reticulation side. It follows that $N^b_1$ and $N^b_2$ have the same leaf sets and that they also share the same set of leaves on each pair of parallel edge sides and on each reticulation side. Moreover, for each pair of parallel edge sides, the allocation of leaves over the two sides is the same in $N_1$ and $N_2$ (and consequently, in $N^b_1$ and $N^b_2$) by \cref{lem:share_sides}b. Lastly, by \cref{lem:ordering}c, the induced $uv$-oriented ordering of the leaves attached to a parallel edge side must be the same in $N_1$ and $N_2$ (and consequently, in $N^b_1$ and $N^b_2$).  It follows that $N^b_1 \cong N^b_2$.
head: environment

label: lem:parallel_contraction
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{lem:parallel_contraction}
    Let $N_1$ and $N_2$ be two simple, $k$-crucial, semi-directed networks on $\mathcal{X}$ with the same generator~$G$ having parallel edge sides. If $N_1$ and $N_2$ are leaf-side consistent and they have isomorphic backbones, then $\mathcal{S}_{k} (N_1 ) \simeq \mathcal{S}_{k} (N_2)$ if and only if $\mathcal{S}_{k} (N^c_1 ) \simeq \mathcal{S}_{k} (N^c_2)$, where $N^c_i$ is the parallel contraction of $N_i$, $i \in \{1, 2\}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathcal{Y} \subseteq \mathcal{X}$ be the set of leaves attached to parallel edge sides of~$N_1$, and $\mathcal{Z} \subseteq \mathcal{X}$ the set of leaves attached to reticulation sides of~$N_1$. Observe that then $\mathcal{Y}$ must also be the set of leaves attached to parallel edge sides of~$N_2$ and $\mathcal{Z}$ must be the set of leaves attached to reticulation sides of~$N_2$, since $N_1$ and $N_2$ are leaf-side consistent.
By \cref{prop:crucial_leaves} and since $\mathcal{Y} \cup \mathcal{Z}$ is a set of crucial leaves of both $N_1$ and $N_2$, the backbones $N^b_1$ and $N^b_2$ of $N_1$ and $N_2$, respectively, have~$G$ as their generator. By assumption, we also have $N^b_1 \cong N^b_2$.
It follows that $N_1$ and $N_2$ have the exact same allocation of leaves in $\mathcal{Z}$ over their reticulation sides and the same allocation of leaves in $\mathcal{Y}$ over their parallel edge sides. 
Moreover, since each parallel edge side~$S = uv$ of~$G$ is directed and therefore oriented, it follows from $N^b_1 \cong N^b_2$ that the $uv$-oriented ordering induced by~$S$ of the set of leaves attached to $S$ must be the same in both $N_1$ and $N_2$. 
This implies that any difference in $k$-nets between $N_1$ and $N_2$ cannot be due to differences in the $uv$-oriented ordering of the attached leaves induced by a parallel edge side.
Hence, such a difference in $k$-nets between $N_1$ and $N_2$ must be witnessed by differences in the $k$-nets of $N^c_1$ and $N^c_2$.
                                                                                                                                                                               
The equivalence stated in the proposition then readily follows.
head: environment

label: lem:level_quarnet
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{lem:level_quarnet}
    Let~$N$ be a strictly level-$k$ semi-directed network and~$3\leq k'\leq k$. Then there exists a $k''$-net of~$N$, with~$k''\leq k'$, that is not level-$(k'-1)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let~$B$ be a strictly level-$k$ blob of~$N$. Let~$N_B$ be the simple strictly level-$k$ semi-directed network obtained from~$N$ by deleting all vertices that are not in~$B$ and not adjacent to a vertex of~$B$. By \cref{lem:excellent_original}, $N_B$ has an excellent cycle~$C_1$. Let~$x_1$ be the leaf adjacent to the sink of~$C_1$ and let~$j=1$. Repeat the following while~$|\{x_1,\ldots ,x_{j}\}|<k'$ and~$U=\cup_{i=1}^{j} C_i$ is not equal to the vertex set~$V(B)$ of~$B$. Let~$e$ be an edge incident to~$U$ (i.e., which has one endpoint in~$U$ and one endpoint not in~$U$) that is not a cut-edge. By \cref{lem:excellent_original}, $N_B$ has an excellent cycle~$C_{j+1}$ containing~$e$. Let~$x_{j+1}$ be the leaf adjacent to the sink of~$C_{j+1}$. Increase~$j$ by~$1$ and repeat. This procedure terminates when $U=\cup_{i=1}^{j} C_i=V(B)$ or~$|\{x_1,\ldots ,x_{j}\}|=k'$ or both. Let $X'=\{x_1,\ldots ,x_{j}\}$.
    
    First suppose $|X'|=k'$. Then~$U$ has~$k'$ sinks and each leaf of~$X'$ is adjacent to a sink of~$U$ in~$N_B$. Hence, the $k'$-net $N_B|_{X'}$ has at least~$k'$ reticulations. Moreover,~$U$ is biconnected by construction. It follows that $N_B|_{X'}$ is simple and not level-$(k'-1)$. Let~$X''$ be a set of~$k'$ leaves of~$N$ containing, for each leaf~$x\in X'$, a leaf~$x'$ of~$N$ that is reachable by a path from~$x$ that is disjoint from~$B$. Then $N|_{X''}$ is a $k'$-net of~$N$ that is not level-$(k'-1)$.

    Now suppose $U=V(B)$ and $|X'|<k'$. Then~$U$ contains exactly~$k$ reticulations. Suppose $N_B|_{X'}$ is strictly level~$\ell < k' \leq k$ and note that $\ell \geq |X'|$ since each leaf in $X'$ is adjacent to a sink. Then~$B$ contains $g \leq k-\ell$ good cycles that each have only two vertices with degree higher than~$2$ (so that these cycles are contracted when constructing $N_B|_{X'}$). Let~$X''$ contain all leaves of~$X'$ and, for $\max \{ g, k' - \ell \}$ good cycles, a leaf incident to that cycle in~$N_B$. Then $N_B|_{X''}$ is a $k''$-net of~$N_B$, with $k'' \leq k'$, that is not level-$(k'-1)$. It then follows, by the same argument as the final argument in the previous case, that there exists a $k''$-net of~$N$ that is not level-$(k'-1)$.
head: environment

title: Proposition

\label{lem:level2_encoding}

label: lem:generator1-17
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:generator1-17}
    Let $N_1$ and $N_2$ be two simple, strictly level-3, semi-directed networks on $\mathcal{X}$ having the same generator~$G$ of type 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 15, 16, or 17. If $\mathcal{S}_{4} (N_1 ) \simeq \mathcal{S}_{4} (N_2)$, then $N_1$ and $N_2$ are isomorphic.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $k$ be the cruciality of $G$ and note that $k \leq 3$ by \cref{obs:level_cruciality}. By \cref{lem:equivalence_class_encoding}, $N_1$ and $N_2$ are leaf-side consistent. We consider four cases, depending on the type of~$G$. Recall that in all cases, $G$ has no parallel edge sides.
    
    \textbf{Case 1:} $G$ is of type 1, 5, 6, or 7. Observe that the following hold for each of these generator types: (i) $k \leq 2$; (ii) each side of~$G$ forms its own equivalence class; (iii) each edge side of~$G$ is oriented. Since $N_1$ and $N_2$ are leaf-side consistent, we may assume by (ii) that each side of~$G$ has the same set of leaves attached to it in both $N_1$ and $N_2$. Combining \cref{lem:ordering}b with (i) and (iii), it follows that each edge side~$S=uv$ of~$G$ induces the same $uv$-oriented ordering of the set of leaves attached to it in both $N_1$ and $N_2$. Thus, $N_1 \cong N_2$.

    \textbf{Case 2:} $G$ is of type 2 or 8. Observe that $k \leq 2$ (in particular, $k=1$ if $G$ is of type 2, and $k=2$ if $G$ is of type 8). Let $S$ be the topmost reticulation side of~$G$ according to the planar representation in \cref{fig:generators} (for type~2, this is the sole reticulation side). Since $N_1$ and $N_2$ are leaf-side consistent, they both have the same leaf~$x\in \mathcal{X}$ attached to~$S$ (Insight~2.1). Denote by $S'=ur$ and $S'' =v r$ the two oriented edge sides of $G$ incident to the reticulation side~$S$. Let $\mathcal{Y}'$ and $\mathcal{Y}''$ be the sets of leaves that are attached to $S'$ and $S''$, respectively, in $N_1$. By \cref{lem:share_sides}, $\mathcal{Y}'$ and $\mathcal{Y}''$ are also the sets of leaves attached to $S'$ and $S''$, respectively, in $N_2$ (Insight~2.2). By \cref{lem:ordering}b, the $ur$-oriented ordering of $\mathcal{Y}'$ induced by $S'$ (respectively, the $vr$-oriented ordering of $\mathcal{Y}''$ induced by $S''$) is the same in $N_1$ and $N_2$ (Insight~2.3). Lastly, for $i=1,2$, put $N_i'\coloneq N_i|_{X\setminus \{x\}}$. Note that $N_i'$ is a level-2, semi-directed network. By \cref{lem:level2_encoding}, $N'_1 \cong N'_2$ (Insight~2.4). Together, Insights~2.1--2.4 show that $N_1 \cong N_2$.

    \textbf{Case 3:} $G$ is of type 15. Observe that $k=3$. Let $S_1$, $S_2$ and $S_3$ denote the reticulation sides of~$G$, ordered from top to bottom and left to right according to the planar representation in \cref{fig:generators}. Let $x, y, z \in \mathcal{X}$ be the leaves attached to $S_1$, $S_2$, and $S_3$, respectively, in~$N_1$. Since $N_1$ and $N_2$ are leaf-side consistent, $x, y, z$ are also attached to $S_1, S_2, S_3$, respectively, in $N_2$ (Insight~3.1). For $i \in \{1,2\}$, put $N'_i \coloneq N_i|_{\mathcal{X} \setminus \{x\}}$. Note that $N'_i$ is a level-2, semi-directed network. By \cref{lem:level2_encoding}, $N'_1 \cong N'_2$ (Insight~3.2). Let $S' = ur$ and $S'' = vr$ be the two oriented edge sides of~$G$ incident to $S_1$. By Insights~3.1 and~3.2, any potential non-isomorphism between $N_1$ and $N_2$ can only arise from a difference in the $ur$-oriented or $vr$-oriented orderings induced by $S'$ or $S''$, respectively, of the leaves attached to them. Now put $N''_i \coloneq N_i|_{\mathcal{X} \setminus \{z\}}$, for $i \in \{1, 2\}$. Note that the oriented edge sides~$S', S''$ correspond to oriented edge sides in $N''_i$. By \cref{lem:level2_encoding} and since $N''_1$ and $N''_2$ are level-2, semi-directed networks, $N''_1 \cong N''_2$. So, the oriented orderings induced by these two sides of the leaves attached to them coincide in $N''_1$ and $N''_2$, and hence also in $N_1$ and $N_2$. It follows that $N_1 \cong N_2$.

    \textbf{Case 4:} $G$ is of type 16 or 17. Observe that (i) $k = 3$; (ii) each side of $G$ forms its own equivalence class; (iii) each edge side is oriented. Since the two networks are leaf-side consistent, each side~$S$ has the same set of leaves~$\mathcal{Y}_S$ attached to it in both $N_1$ and $N_2$. So, by (ii), any potential non-isomorphism between $N_1$ and $N_2$ can only arise from some edge side~$S$ (which is oriented by (iii)) having a different induced oriented ordering of $\mathcal{Y}_S$ in $N_1$ and $N_2$. Note that for each such edge side~$S$, there is one leaf~$z$ attached to a reticulation side in both $N_1$ and $N_2$, such that the leaves in $\mathcal{Y}_S$ are still attached to an oriented side~$S'$ in $N'_1 \coloneq N_1|_{\mathcal{X} \setminus \{z\}}$ and $N'_2 \coloneq N_2|_{\mathcal{X} \setminus \{z\}}$. Since $N'_1$ and $N'_2$ are level-2, semi-directed networks, we get $N'_1 \cong N'_2$ by \cref{lem:level2_encoding}. Thus, the oriented orderings of $\mathcal{Y}_S$ induced by $S'$ coincide in $N'_1$ and $N'_2$. Hence, the oriented orderings of $\mathcal{Y}_S$ induced by~$S$ also coincide in $N_1$ and $N_2$. Therefore, $N_1 \cong N_2$.

label: lem:generator14
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
As observed at the beginning of this section, the cruciality of~$G$ is 3. Moreover, each of its sides forms its own side-equivalence class, and each edge side is oriented.
    
    (a) Suppose that $\mathcal{S}_{4} (N_1 ) \simeq \mathcal{S}_{4} (N_2)$. By \cref{lem:equivalence_class_encoding}, $N_1$ and $N_2$ are leaf-side consistent---and thus each side of~$G$ has the same leaves attached to it in both $N_1$ and $N_2$. By \cref{lem:ordering}a, the unoriented orderings induced by each edge side of $G$ of the leaves attached to it are the same in $N_1$ and $N_2$. In particular, this means that the unoriented ordering induced by the top side of~$G$ of the leaves attached to it is the same in $N_1$ and $N_2$. Let~$S$ be an edge side that is not the top side of~$G$ and let $\mathcal{Y}_S$ be the set of leaves attached to $S$ in $N_1$ and $N_2$. Observe that $S$ is oriented and that there is a leaf~$z \in \mathcal{X}$ attached to a reticulation side of~$G$ such that the 
    leaves in $\mathcal{Y}_S$ are still attached to an oriented side~$S'$ in $N'_1 \coloneq N_1|_{\mathcal{X} \setminus \{z\}}$ 
    and $N'_2 \coloneq N_2|_{\mathcal{X} \setminus \{z\}}$. Since $N'_1$ and $N'_2$ are level-2, semi-directed networks, we have $N'_1 \cong N'_2$ by \cref{lem:level2_encoding}. Thus, the oriented orderings of $\mathcal{Y}_S$ induced by $S'$ coincide in $N'_1$ and $N'_2$. Hence, the oriented orderings of $\mathcal{Y}_S$ induced by $S$ also coincide in $N_1$ and $N_2$. It follows that $N_1$ and $N_2$ are isomorphic modulo reversing the top side.

    (b) Suppose that $\mathcal{S}_{5} (N_1 ) \simeq \mathcal{S}_{5} (N_2)$. This implies that $\mathcal{S}_{4} (N_1 ) \simeq \mathcal{S}_{4} (N_2)$, so $N_1$ and $N_2$ are isomorphic modulo reversing the top side. By \cref{lem:ordering}b, the induced oriented orderings of the leaves attached to the top side of~$G$ are also the same for $N_1$ and $N_2$. Hence, $N_1 \cong N_2$.

label: thm:main-encoding
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For~(a), first observe that reversing the top side of a type~14 blob leaves the quarnets unchanged. This is easily verified from \cref{fig:counterexample} for a simple network with a single type~14 blob, and the general case follows.

    Also observe that, by \cref{lem:level_quarnet}, a network not in $\mathcal{L}_3$ cannot have the same quarnets (or quinnets) as a network in $\mathcal{L}_3$. Hence, to show the claimed encoding results, it suffices to consider two 
    semi-directed networks $N_1$ and $N_2$ on $\mathcal{X}$ from the class $\mathcal{L}_3$.
    
    (a) Suppose that $\mathcal{S}_{4} (N_1 ) \simeq \mathcal{S}_{4} (N_2)$. Let $B_1$ be an arbitrary blob of $N_1$. As above, observe that the removal of~$B_1$ induces a partition $\{X_1, \ldots, X_m\}$ of the leaf set $\mathcal{X}$ (with $m \geq 3$, $\mathcal{X}=\bigcup_{1 \leq i \leq m} X_i$, $X_i \subseteq \mathcal{X}$ and $X_i \cap X_j = \emptyset$, $1 \le  i \neq j \le m$). By \cref{prop:tree_of_blobs_encoding}, $N_1$ and $N_2$ have isomorphic trees-of-blobs, so there also exists a corresponding blob~$B_2$ of $N_2$ that induces the same partition of $\mathcal{X}$. Pick a set of leaves~$\{x_1, \ldots, x_m \}$ such that $x_i \in X_i$ for each $1 \leq i \leq m$. Put $N'_1 \coloneq N_1|_{\{x_1, \ldots, x_m \}}$ and $N'_2 \coloneq N_2|_{\{x_1, \ldots, x_m \}}$. Since we chose an arbitrary blob~$B_1$ of $N_1$, it now suffices to show that $N'_1$ and $N'_2$ are isomorphic modulo reversing the top side of the type~14 blobs.

    Observe that $N'_1$ and $N'_2$ are simple and that their cruciality is at most~3 (\cref{obs:level_cruciality}). By \cref{cor:generator_encoding}, they have the same generator~$G$. By \cref{lem:equivalence_class_encoding}, $N'_1$ and $N'_2$ are leaf-side consistent. By combining \cref{lem:backbone,lem:parallel_contraction}, we may assume that $N'_1$ and~$N'_2$ are their own parallel contraction or, equivalently, that~$G$ contains no parallel edge sides. If $N'_1$ and $N'_2$ are level-2, the result follows from \cref{lem:level2_encoding}, so we may assume that the two networks are strictly level-3. If $G$ is of type 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 15, 16, or~17, $N'_1$ and $N'_2$ are isomorphic by \cref{lem:generator1-17}. If~$G$ is of type~14, the two networks are isomorphic modulo reversing the top side by \cref{lem:generator14}a. This proves Part~(a).

    (b) Suppose that $\mathcal{S}_{5} (N_1 ) \simeq \mathcal{S}_{5} (N_2)$, which implies $\mathcal{S}_{4} (N_1 ) \simeq \mathcal{S}_{4} (N_2)$. The proof is analogous to the proof of Part~(a) but using \cref{lem:generator14}b instead of \cref{lem:generator14}a when~$G$ is of type~14.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: If a network has fewer than four (respectively, five) leaves, then it possesses no quarnets (respectively, quinnets). Recall from the definition of encoding in \cref{sec:prelims} that, whenever a network has fewer than $k$ leaves, encoding by $k$-nets is understood to mean encoding by its $n$-nets, where $n$ is the number of leaves. Thus, in \cref{thm:main-encoding}, a network in $\mathcal{L}_3$ with fewer than five leaves is understood to be encoded by its unique subnetwork on all of its leaves.
head: environment
